qs.q: Why must BOTH copies of a tumor suppressor gene be lost for tumor development, unlike oncogenes which require mutation of only one allele?
o: The remaining normal allele can still produce functional protein
qs.e: This follows Knudson's two-hit hypothesis. One functional copy of a tumor suppressor gene is sufficient for normal function, so both must be lost. Oncogenes are gain-of-function mutations where one mutant copy is sufficient.

qs.q: In the adenoma-carcinoma sequence of colon cancer, what is the significance of loss of the tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 18q?
o: It occurs first in the sequence
It occurs in the middle stages between KRAS and TP53 mutations
It is not relevant to colon cancer
qs.e: The multistep progression typically follows: APC loss → KRAS activation → 18q loss → TP53 loss. The 18q loss occurs in intermediate stages of progression.

qs.q: Which tumor suppressor gene can trigger apoptosis in response to DNA damage?
o: It acts as the "guardian of the genome" and induces pro-apoptotic proteins like Bax.
qs.e: p53 is activated by DNA damage and can induce cell cycle arrest for repair or trigger apoptosis if damage is irreparable. It acts as the "guardian of the genome" and induces pro-apoptotic proteins like Bax.

qs.q: What protein does the NF2 tumor suppressor gene produce?
qs.e: The NF2 tumor suppressor gene produces neurofibromin-2 (merlin), which facilitates E-cadherin-mediated contact inhibition.

qs.q: What is the fundamental characteristic of tumor suppressor genes?
o: They have no effect on cell growth
They apply brakes to cell proliferation
qs.e: The proteins encoded by tumor suppressor genes apply brakes to cell proliferation. Disruptions of such genes render cells refractory to growth inhibition.
qs.s: TUMOR SUPPRESSOR GENES & CELL CYCLE CONTROL MCQs

qs.q: How many copies of a tumor suppressor gene must be dysfunctional for tumor development?
qs.e: Unlike oncogenes (which require only one mutated copy), both copies of a tumor suppressor gene must be dysfunctional for tumor development to occur.

qs.q: Why must BOTH copies of a tumor suppressor gene be lost for tumor development, unlike oncogenes?
o: Tumor suppressors function like 'brakes'; one working copy is often sufficient
Oncogenes are only found in viruses
qs.e: Tumor suppressor genes usually show a 'recessive' pattern at the cellular level (Knudson's Two-Hit Hypothesis), meaning one functional allele can still control the cell cycle.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Tumor suppressor genes act as cellular brakes, stopping division, repairing DNA, and triggering apoptosis. When both alleles are lost or silenced, unchecked proliferation leads to cancer. Clinicians must recognize how genetic loss drives disease and guide targeted therapy.

sections.p: Tumor suppressor genes (TSGs) encode proteins that inhibit cell cycle progression, promote DNA repair, and induce apoptosis. Diagnosis involves detecting loss of function by mutation, deletion, or epigenetic silencing, often using sequencing, copy‑number analysis, or methylation assays.
b: Loss of function removes cellular brakes
Both alleles must be affected (Knudson two‑hit hypothesis)

t.b: Detects pathogenic mutations in TSGs; a pathogenic variant suggests loss of function.
Identifies deletions/duplications of TSGs; a deletion confirms loss of one allele.
Detects promoter hypermethylation silencing TSGs; hypermethylation indicates functional loss.

sections.p: TSG loss is a foundational event in tumorigenesis; severity is gauged by tumor stage and grade, not by the gene alone. Inherited germline mutations (e.g., BRCA1/2) confer high lifetime risk and influence surveillance strategies.

t.b: Assesses tumor size, nodal involvement, metastasis; guides treatment intensity.
Evaluates differentiation; high grade suggests aggressive biology.

sections.p: The primary cause is genetic alteration: point mutations, deletions, or epigenetic silencing. Environmental factors (radiation, carcinogens) can induce DNA damage that overwhelms TSG repair capacity.
b: Point mutations in p53, RB, BRCA1/2

t.b: Radiation or carcinogen exposure increases DNA damage; if TSG repair fails, cancer risk rises.

sections.p: Clinical presentation mirrors the tumor type rather than the gene itself. For example, BRCA mutations present as breast or ovarian cancer; TSC1/2 loss causes tuberous sclerosis with skin, renal, and CNS lesions.
b: Family history may hint at inherited TSG mutations

sections.p: Investigations focus on tumor type and TSG status. When TSG testing is unavailable, rely on histology and immunohistochemistry to infer loss of function.

t.b: Detects protein accumulation; strong nuclear staining suggests p53 mutation.
Identifies gene deletions; loss of signal indicates deletion.

sections.p: Red flags include rapid tumor growth, early metastasis, or unusual histology. Complications arise from unchecked proliferation: invasion, metastasis, and treatment resistance.

t.b: Detects invasion into adjacent structures; invasion indicates aggressive disease.
Identifies skeletal metastasis; early metastasis requires systemic therapy.

sections.p: Management targets the underlying TSG loss and the tumor. For BRCA‑mutated cancers, PARP inhibitors exploit synthetic lethality. Other TSG‑driven tumors use standard cytotoxic or targeted agents, with surgery or radiation as needed.

t.b: Treats tumors with BRCA loss; blocks DNA repair, leading to tumor cell death.
Used when targeted options are unavailable; cytotoxic agents kill rapidly dividing cells.

sections.p: Surveillance depends on inherited TSG risk. For BRCA carriers, regular imaging and risk‑reducing surgery are options. Lifestyle modifications reduce secondary DNA damage.

t.b: Prophylactic mastectomy or oophorectomy lowers cancer incidence in high‑risk individuals.
Smoking cessation and sun protection reduce DNA damage that could overwhelm TSG repair.

sections.p: TSG loss is often mistaken for oncogene activation. Both lead to proliferation but via different mechanisms. Also, epigenetic silencing can mimic gene deletion.

t.b: Identifies activating mutations; absence suggests TSG involvement.

sections.p: Low‑level mosaicism or subclonal mutations may escape detection. Immunohistochemistry can show overexpression even when the gene is intact.

t.b: Detects low‑frequency mutations that standard panels miss.

whenToSeekHelp: New neurological deficits in a patient with known TSG mutation
Unexplained anemia or bleeding in a patient with a history of TSG‑related cancer

faq.q: What is the difference between an oncogene and a tumor suppressor gene?
faq.a: Oncogenes are overactive drivers of proliferation; tumor suppressor genes normally inhibit growth and must be inactivated for cancer to develop.

faq.q: Can lifestyle changes prevent TSG‑related cancers?
faq.a: Yes, reducing exposure to carcinogens and maintaining healthy habits can lower DNA damage that overwhelms TSG repair.

faq.q: Why are PARP inhibitors effective in BRCA‑mutated cancers?
faq.a: They block an alternative DNA repair pathway; cells lacking BRCA cannot repair DNA, leading to cell death.
